claims.evidence: This is a finding from the temporal analysis of neural representations in the study.

claims.claim: Perception requires probabilistic inference to resolve the uncertain causes of essentially ambiguous sensory input.
claims.source: Whilst perception typically feels effortless and automatic, it requires probabilistic inference to resolve the uncertain causes of essentially ambiguous sensory input (Helmholtz, 1856).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Helmholtz (1856), representing established theory in perception.

claims.claim: Human observers are capable of discriminating which perceptual decisions are more likely to be correct using subjective feelings of confidence.
claims.source: Human observers are capable of discriminating which perceptual decisions are more likely to be correct using subjective feelings of confidence (Pollack and Decker, 1958).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pollack and Decker (1958), representing established empirical findings.

claims.claim: Feelings of perceptual confidence have been associated with metacognitive processes.
claims.source: These feelings of perceptual confidence have been associated with metacognitive processes (Fleming and Daw, 2017) that enable self-monitoring for learning (Veenman et al., 2004) and communication (Bahrami et al., 2012; Frith, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to Fleming and Daw (2017), Veenman et al. (2004), Bahrami et al. (2012), and Frith (2012).

claims.claim: Metacognitive processes enable self-monitoring for learning.
claims.source: These feelings of perceptual confidence have been associated with metacognitive processes (Fleming and Daw, 2017) that enable self-monitoring for learning (Veenman et al., 2004) and communication (Bahrami et al., 2012; Frith, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Veenman et al. (2004).

claims.claim: Metacognitive processes enable communication.
claims.source: These feelings of perceptual confidence have been associated with metacognitive processes (Fleming and Daw, 2017) that enable self-monitoring for learning (Veenman et al., 2004) and communication (Bahrami et al., 2012; Frith, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Bahrami et al. (2012) and Frith (2012).

claims.claim: Perceptual decisions are described by sequential sampling processes at the computational level.
claims.source: At the computational level, perceptual decisions are described by sequential sampling processes (Ratcliff, 1978; Vickers, 1970), in which noisy samples of evidence are accumulated over time, until there is sufficient evidence to commit to a decision.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Ratcliff (1978) and Vickers (1970), representing established computational models.

claims.claim: In sequential sampling processes, noisy samples of evidence are accumulated over time until there is sufficient evidence to commit to a decision.
claims.source: At the computational level, perceptual decisions are described by sequential sampling processes (Ratcliff, 1978; Vickers, 1970), in which noisy samples of evidence are accumulated over time, until there is sufficient evidence to commit to a decision.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the sequential sampling framework supported by the cited references.

claims.claim: The most relevant information for evaluating perceptual confidence is the quantity and quality of evidence used to make the perceptual decision.
claims.source: The most relevant information for evaluating perceptual confidence is the quantity and quality of evidence used to make the perceptual decision (Kepecs et al., 2008; Moreno-Bote, 2010; Vickers, 1979).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Kepecs et al. (2008), Moreno-Bote (2010), and Vickers (1979).

claims.claim: Confidence can be reliably predicted from the firing rates of neurons coding the perceptual decision itself.
claims.source: Indeed, confidence (or a non-human primate proxy for confidence) can be reliably predicted from the firing rates of neurons coding the perceptual decision itself (Kiani and Shadlen, 2009), suggesting that confidence may be a direct by-product of perceptual processing.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kiani and Shadlen (2009), representing empirical findings from neurophysiology.

claims.claim: Confidence may be a direct by-product of perceptual processing.
claims.source: Indeed, confidence (or a non-human primate proxy for confidence) can be reliably predicted from the firing rates of neurons coding the perceptual decision itself (Kiani and Shadlen, 2009), suggesting that confidence may be a direct by-product of perceptual processing.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited neurophysiological findings.

claims.claim: Confidence can integrate additional evidence after the observer commits to their perceptual decision.
claims.source: Confidence can integrate additional evidence after the observer commits to their perceptual decision (Pleskac and Busemeyer, 2010; Baranski and Petrusic, 1994), and while this continued evidence accumulation could incorporate only perceptual information, it implies that confidence evaluation does not directly follow from perceptual decision commitment (and therefore involves at least partially dissociable neural processes).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Pleskac and Busemeyer (2010) and Baranski and Petrusic (1994).

claims.claim: Confidence evaluation does not directly follow from perceptual decision commitment.
claims.source: Confidence can integrate additional evidence after the observer commits to their perceptual decision (Pleskac and Busemeyer, 2010; Baranski and Petrusic, 1994), and while this continued evidence accumulation could incorporate only perceptual information, it implies that confidence evaluation does not directly follow from perceptual decision commitment (and therefore involves at least partially dissociable neural processes).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited behavioral findings about post-decisional evidence integration.

claims.claim: Confidence evaluation involves at least partially dissociable neural processes from perceptual decision-making.
claims.source: Confidence can integrate additional evidence after the observer commits to their perceptual decision (Pleskac and Busemeyer, 2010; Baranski and Petrusic, 1994), and while this continued evidence accumulation could incorporate only perceptual information, it implies that confidence evaluation does not directly follow from perceptual decision commitment (and therefore involves at least partially dissociable neural processes).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral evidence of post-decisional integration.

claims.claim: Perceptual confidence can rely on separate non-perceptual sources of information such as decision time.
claims.source: There is also evidence that perceptual confidence can rely on separate (non-perceptual) sources of information, such as decision time (Kiani et al., 2014) and attentional cues (Denison et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kiani et al. (2014).

claims.claim: Perceptual confidence can rely on separate non-perceptual sources of information such as attentional cues.
claims.source: There is also evidence that perceptual confidence can rely on separate (non-perceptual) sources of information, such as decision time (Kiani et al., 2014) and attentional cues (Denison et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Denison et al. (2018).

claims.claim: Confidence precision is correlated across different cognitive tasks such as memory and perception.
claims.source: Indeed, there is some evidence that confidence precision is correlated across different cognitive tasks (such as memory and perception; Mazancieux et al., 2020), suggesting a common source of noise affecting the computation of confidence across tasks (on top of the sensory noise; Bang et al., 2019; Shekhar and Rahnev, 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mazancieux et al. (2020).

claims.claim: There is a common source of noise affecting the computation of confidence across tasks on top of sensory noise.
claims.source: Indeed, there is some evidence that confidence precision is correlated across different cognitive tasks (such as memory and perception; Mazancieux et al., 2020), suggesting a common source of noise affecting the computation of confidence across tasks (on top of the sensory noise; Bang et al., 2019; Shekhar and Rahnev, 2021).
claims.evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to Bang et al. (2019) and Shekhar and Rahnev (2021).

claims.claim: Modulations in confidence have been linked with activity in subregions of the prefrontal cortex including the orbitofrontal cortex.
claims.source: Several experiments have linked modulations in confidence with activity in a variety of subregions of the prefrontal cortex (including the orbitofrontal cortex, Lak et al., 2014; Masset et al., 2020; right frontopolar cortex, Yokoyama et al., 2010; rostro-lateral prefrontal cortex, Fleming et al., 2012; Geurts et al., 2021; Cortese et al., 2016; see also Vaccaro and Fleming, 2018, for a meta-analysis).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Lak et al. (2014) and Masset et al. (2020).

claims.claim: Modulations in confidence have been linked with activity in the right frontopolar cortex.
claims.source: Several experiments have linked modulations in confidence with activity in a variety of subregions of the prefrontal cortex (including the orbitofrontal cortex, Lak et al., 2014; Masset et al., 2020; right frontopolar cortex, Yokoyama et al., 2010; rostro-lateral prefrontal cortex, Fleming et al., 2012; Geurts et al., 2021; Cortese et al., 2016; see also Vaccaro and Fleming, 2018, for a meta-analysis).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yokoyama et al. (2010).

claims.claim: Modulations in confidence have been linked with activity in the rostro-lateral prefrontal cortex.
claims.source: Several experiments have linked modulations in confidence with activity in a variety of subregions of the prefrontal cortex (including the orbitofrontal cortex, Lak et al., 2014; Masset et al., 2020; right frontopolar cortex, Yokoyama et al., 2010; rostro-lateral prefrontal cortex, Fleming et al., 2012; Geurts et al., 2021; Cortese et al., 2016; see also Vaccaro and Fleming, 2018, for a meta-analysis).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Fleming et al. (2012), Geurts et al. (2021), and Cortese et al. (2016).

claims.claim: Disrupting processing in subregions of the prefrontal cortex tends to impair the ability to appropriately adjust behavioural confidence responses whilst leaving perceptual decision accuracy largely unaffected.
claims.source: Moreover, disrupting the processing in subregions of the prefrontal cortex (Fleming et al., 2014; Lak et al., 2014; Rounis et al., 2010) tends to impair (though not obliterate) the ability to appropriately adjust behavioural confidence responses, whilst leaving perceptual decision accuracy largely unaffected (although these results can be difficult to replicate, Bor et al., 2017; Lapate et al., 2020, and may not generalise to metacognition for memory; Fleming et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Fleming et al. (2014), Lak et al. (2014), and Rounis et al. (2010), with caveats noted from Bor et al. (2017) and Lapate et al. (2020).

claims.claim: Post-decisional changes in confidence magnitude correlate with signals from the posterior medial frontal cortex.
claims.source: These studies show that post-decisional changes in confidence magnitude correlate with signals from the posterior medial frontal cortex.
claims.evidence: This refers to findings from studies mentioned in the preceding sentence (Fleming et al., 2018; Murphy et al., 2015).

claims.claim: Error signals drive medial frontal activity more strongly than decision accuracy.
claims.source: However, these signals could reflect processes occurring downstream of confidence, such as an emotional response to the error signal, which has been shown to drive medial frontal activity more strongly than decision accuracy (Gehring and Willoughby, 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gehring and Willoughby (2002).

claims.claim: Perceptual decision sensitivity (d') was significantly decreased with two fewer stimuli in the Less condition compared to the Free task.
claims.source: Replicating these previous results (Balsdon et al., 2020), we found that perceptual decision sensitivity (d') was significantly decreased with just two fewer stimuli in the Less condition compared to those same (pmin) trials in the Free task (Wilcoxon sign rank Z = 3.88, p < 0.001, Bonferroni corrected for three comparisons), but four additional stimuli in the More condition resulted in only a small but not significant increase compared to the pmax trials in the Free task (Z = -1.53, p = 0.13, uncorrected).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral analysis of the current study.

claims.claim: Four additional stimuli in the More condition resulted in only a small but not significant increase in perceptual decision sensitivity compared to the Free task.
claims.source: Replicating these previous results (Balsdon et al., 2020), we found that perceptual decision sensitivity (d') was significantly decreased with just two fewer stimuli in the Less condition compared to those same (pmin) trials in the Free task (Wilcoxon sign rank Z = 3.88, p < 0.001, Bonferroni corrected for three comparisons), but four additional stimuli in the More condition resulted in only a small but not significant increase compared to the pmax trials in the Free task (Z = -1.53, p = 0.13, uncorrected).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral analysis of the current study.

claims.claim: Cross-validated model comparison provided significant evidence that observers were implementing a covert bound.
claims.source: Cross-validated model comparison provided significant evidence that observers were implementing a covert bound (mean relative increase in model log-likelihood = 0.048, bootstrapped p = 0.001, Figure 2c).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling analysis, with reference to Figure 2c.

claims.claim: There was no evidence that observers were implementing a covert bound on confidence.
claims.source: In contrast to what we found for the perceptual decision, there was no evidence that observers were implementing a covert bound on confidence: Implementing the same bound as the perceptual decision did not improve the fit (relative improvement with bound = −0.007, bootstrapped p = 0.11, uncorrected) and an independent bound actually significantly reduced the fit compared to continued accumulation (relative improvement = −0.014, p = 0.022, Bonferroni corrected for two comparisons; Figure 2c).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling analysis, with reference to Figure 2c.

claims.claim: The best description of both perceptual and confidence responses was provided by a partially dissociated computational architecture where perceptual and confidence decisions are based on the same noisy representation of the sensory evidence, but confidence accumulation incurs additional noise and can continue after the completion of perceptual decision processes.
claims.source: The best description of both perceptual and confidence responses was provided by a partially dissociated computational architecture (full details in Appendix 1), where perceptual and confidence decisions are based on the same noisy representation of the sensory evidence, but confidence accumulation incurs additional noise and can continue after the completion of perceptual decision processes (Figure 2d, and the predictions of this model for individual participants are show in Figure 2e).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling analysis, with references to Figures 2d and 2e.

claims.claim: The presented evidence accumulated over all samples explains substantial variance in observers' perceptual decisions.
claims.source: First, we find the presented evidence accumulated over all samples does explain substantial variance in observers' perceptual decisions (average β = 0.77, t(19) = 6.48, p < 0.001), and confidence evaluations (with the evidence signed by the perceptual response; β = 0.24, t(19) = 6.46, p < 0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the GLM analysis of the current study.

claims.claim: The presented evidence accumulated over all samples explains substantial variance in observers' confidence evaluations.
claims.source: First, we find the presented evidence accumulated over all samples does explain substantial variance in observers' perceptual decisions (average β = 0.77, t(19) = 6.48, p < 0.001), and confidence evaluations (with the evidence signed by the perceptual response; β = 0.24, t(19) = 6.46, p < 0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the GLM analysis of the current study.

claims.claim: The total accumulated evidence in the More condition was not a significantly better predictor of observers' perceptual decisions than the evidence up to four samples prior to the response.
claims.source: Second, the total accumulated evidence in the More condition was not a significantly better predictor of the observers' perceptual decisions than the evidence up to four samples prior to the response (average difference in β = 0.034, t(19) = 1.63, p = 0.12), while for the Same and Less conditions the total accumulated evidence was a significantly better predictor (Less: t(19) = 4.99, p < 0.001; Same: t(19) = 3.11, p = 0.006; causing a significant interaction between condition and sample accumulated to F(2,38) = 10.348, p = 0.001, Bonferroni corrected for three comparisons, Figure 2f, top).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the GLM analysis, with reference to Figure 2f.

claims.claim: For the Same and Less conditions, the total accumulated evidence was a significantly better predictor of perceptual decisions than evidence accumulated to four samples prior.
claims.source: Second, the total accumulated evidence in the More condition was not a significantly better predictor of the observers' perceptual decisions than the evidence up to four samples prior to the response (average difference in β = 0.034, t(19) = 1.63, p = 0.12), while for the Same and Less conditions the total accumulated evidence was a significantly better predictor (Less: t(19) = 4.99, p < 0.001; Same: t(19) = 3.11, p = 0.006; causing a significant interaction between condition and sample accumulated to F(2,38) = 10.348, p = 0.001, Bonferroni corrected for three comparisons, Figure 2f, top).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the GLM analysis, with reference to Figure 2f.

claims.claim: The accumulated evidence up to the final sample in the More condition was a significantly better predictor of confidence than the evidence accumulated to four samples from the response.
claims.source: Rather, the accumulated evidence up to the final sample in the More condition was a significantly better predictor of confidence than the evidence accumulated to four samples from the response (average difference in β = 0.26, t(19) = 5.33, p < 0.001), supporting the prediction from the computational model analysis that observers integrated all the presented evidence for evaluating confidence.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the GLM analysis of the current study.

claims.claim: Spectral power in the 8 to 32 Hz frequency range could be used to classify perceptual decisions based on lateralised differences over motor cortex.
claims.source: Initial analysis suggested the spectral power in the 8 to 32 Hz frequency range (the 'alpha' and 'beta' bands) could be used to classify perceptual decisions based on lateralised differences over motor cortex (Appendix 5).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the EEG spectral analysis of the current study.

claims.claim: Training around −0.78 to 0.44 s from the time of the response in the Free task led to significantly better accuracy testing in the More condition than in the Less condition, prior to when the response was entered.
claims.source: Statistical comparison revealed substantial clusters of significant differences (Figure 3b): Training around −0.78 to 0.44 s from the time of the response in the Free task led to significantly better accuracy testing in the More condition than in the Less condition, prior to when the response was entered (for the cluster testing at −2.5 to −1.6 s Zave = 2.04, pcluster = 0.002; testing at −1.5 to −1 s, Zave = 1.95, pcluster = 0.01; testing at −0.8 to −0.3, Zave = 2.32, pcluster < 0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the cross-classification analysis, with reference to Figure 3b.

claims.claim: Observers were not only committing to their perceptual decision early, but already preparing their motor response.
claims.source: This pattern of findings suggests that observers were not only committing to their perceptual decision early, but already preparing their motor response.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cross-classification analysis results.

claims.claim: The optimal evidence L accumulated over all samples could predict the strength of the classifier prediction at response time.
claims.source: We found that the optimal evidence L, accumulated over all samples, could predict the strength of the classifier prediction at response time (mean β = 0.11, t(19) = 3.89, p < 0.001; Figure 3c).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the exploratory analysis, with reference to Figure 3c.

claims.claim: In the More condition, the evidence accumulated up to four samples prior to the response still predicted the strength of the classifier prediction.
claims.source: But, in the More condition, the evidence accumulated up to four samples prior to the response still predicted the strength of the classifier prediction (t(19) = 3.81, p = 0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the exploratory analysis of the current study.

claims.claim: There was a significant interaction between condition and samples accumulated in predicting the strength of the classifier prediction.
claims.source: This difference between conditions over samples is evidenced by a significant interaction based on a repeated measures ANOVA (F(8,152) = 2.429, p = 0.05, after Bonferroni correction for three comparisons).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the exploratory analysis of the current study.

claims.claim: The optimal observer must encode the orientation of the stimulus, estimate the decision update based on the categories, and add this to the accumulated evidence for discriminating between the categories.
claims.source: To perform this task the optimal observer must encode the orientation of the stimulus, estimate the decision update based on the categories, and add this to the accumulated evidence for discriminating between the categories (Wyart et al., 2012; Wyart et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the optimal computation supported by citations to Wyart et al. (2012, 2015).

claims.claim: The precision of the representations of stimulus orientation, momentary decision update, and accumulated evidence showed distinct time courses and relied on distinct patterns of EEG activity over scalp topography.
claims.source: The precision of the representations of these variables showed distinct time courses and relied on distinct patterns of EEG activity over scalp topography (Figure 4b).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the EEG encoding analysis, with reference to Figure 4b.

claims.claim: There was a transient representation of stimulus orientation localised over occipital electrodes.
claims.source: There was a transient representation of stimulus orientation localised over occipital electrodes.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the EEG encoding analysis of the current study.

claims.claim: The representation of the momentary decision update was maintained for a longer duration, initially supported by occipital electrodes, then increasingly localised over central-parietal electrodes.
claims.source: The representation of the momentary decision update was maintained for a longer duration, initially supported by occipital electrodes, then increasingly localised over central-parietal electrodes.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the EEG encoding analysis of the current study.

claims.claim: The representation of the accumulated evidence was sustained even longer and relied on both frontal and occipital electrodes.
claims.source: The representation of the accumulated evidence was sustained even longer and relied on both frontal and occipital electrodes.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the EEG encoding analysis of the current study.

claims.claim: The precision of the representation of stimulus orientation did not significantly vary based on whether behaviour matched the optimal response.
claims.source: For each variable, we estimated the representation precision separately for epochs leading to behavioural responses that differed from the optimal response (based on L), and responses that matched those of the optimal observer (Replay task epochs only; Figure 4c; Appendix 3). For perceptual decisions, the optimal observer responds with the correct category. For confidence evaluations, the optimal observer gives high confidence on trials with greater than the median evidence (over all trials) for their perceptual response. The precision of the representation of stimulus orientation did not significantly vary based on whether behaviour matched the optimal response.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral comparison analysis, with reference to Figure 4c.

claims.claim: The representation precision of the momentary decision update showed a significant effect for the perceptual decision from 380 to 468 ms.
claims.source: The representation precision of the momentary decision update showed a significant effect for the perceptual decision from 380 to 468 ms (Favg(1,19) = 7.97, pcluster = 0.008) and a significant interaction between perceptual and confidence responses from 396 to 468 ms (Favg(1,19) = 6.66, pcluster = 0.022) and from 716 to 856 ms (Favg(1,19) = 10.75, pcluster < 0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral comparison analysis of the current study.

claims.claim: Representation precision of accumulated evidence was significantly reduced in epochs leading to non-optimal perceptual decisions from 108 ms post stimulus onset to the end of the epoch.
claims.source: Representation precision was significantly reduced in epochs leading to non-optimal perceptual decisions from 108 ms post stimulus onset to the end of the epoch (Favg(1,19) = 13.65, pcluster <0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral comparison analysis of the current study.

claims.claim: There was a significant interaction between perceptual and confidence responses in the representation precision of accumulated evidence from 696 to 836 ms.
claims.source: In addition, there was a significant interaction with confidence from 696 to 836 ms (Favg(1,19) = 8.72, pcluster = 0.005).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the behavioral comparison analysis of the current study.

claims.claim: The precision of the early representation of accumulated evidence was significantly attenuated for the last four samples of the More condition compared to the last four samples of the Less condition.
claims.source: Indeed, the precision of the early representation of accumulated evidence was significantly attenuated for the last four samples of the More condition (in which observers were likely to have already committed to a decision), compared to the last four samples of the Less condition (where observers were unlikely to have committed to a decision; from the start of the epoch to 424 ms, Figure 4d; tavg(19) = −5.19, pcluster<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the condition comparison analysis, with reference to Figure 4d.

claims.claim: Differences in representation precision between More and Less conditions were not present for the encoding of stimulus orientation nor the decision update.
claims.source: These differences in representation precision were not present for the encoding of stimulus orientation, nor the decision update, suggesting that these processes may reflect input to perceptual evidence accumulation, but not the accumulation process itself.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the condition comparison analysis of the current study.

claims.claim: Signals related to internal evidence for perceptual decisions were initially clustered over posterior electrodes, becoming dispersed over more anterior electrodes late in the epoch.
claims.source: For perceptual decision-making, signals related to L* were initially clustered over posterior electrodes, becoming dispersed over more anterior electrodes late in the epoch (Figure 5a, top).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the Bayesian scan statistics analysis, with reference to Figure 5a.

claims.claim: For confidence, two co-temporal clusters in posterior and anterior electrodes emerged from 668 ms to 824 ms from stimulus onset.
claims.source: For confidence, we found two co-temporal clusters in posterior and anterior electrodes emerging from 668 ms to 824 ms from stimulus onset (Figure 5a, bottom).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the Bayesian scan statistics analysis, with reference to Figure 5a.

claims.claim: An early posterior cluster of signals was strongly related to internal evidence for perceptual decisions but was not diagnostic of confidence evaluations.
claims.source: In Figure 5a, we highlight an early posterior cluster of signals strongly related to L* for perceptual decisions, that was not diagnostic of confidence evaluations (in fact the evidence was in favour of the null hypothesis; summed log likelihood ratio = −1176).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the Bayesian scan statistics analysis, with reference to Figure 5a.

claims.claim: Combining the perceptual and confidence clusters improves the representation precision.
claims.source: That the information from these clusters is not redundant is evident from the fact that combining the clusters improves the representation precision (Figure 5b).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the cluster analysis, with reference to Figure 5b.

claims.claim: The representation precision of the early posterior cluster was attenuated for the last four samples of the More condition.
claims.source: Similar to the previous analysis (Figure 4d), the representation precision of the early posterior cluster was attenuated for the last four samples of the More condition.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the cluster analysis of the current study.

claims.claim: The representation precision of the confidence cluster was maintained for the last four samples of the More condition.
claims.source: But, the representation precision of the confidence cluster was maintained (a repeated measures ANOVA revealed a significant interaction between cluster and condition for decoding precision in the last four samples, F(1,19) = 32.00, p = 0.001, Bonferroni corrected for three comparisons).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the cluster analysis of the current study.

claims.claim: The estimate of single-sample inference error from the confidence cluster representation was significantly correlated with the single-sample inference error estimated from the computational model of confidence ratings.
claims.source: This estimate of the single-sample inference error was significantly correlated with the single-sample inference error estimated from the computational model of confidence ratings (t(19) = 5.12, p < 0.001), and this correlation was significantly greater than the correlation with the error estimated from the model of perceptual decisions alone (t(19) = 2.62, p = 0.017; see Appendix 8).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the model comparison analysis of the current study.

claims.claim: Noise Max epochs showed a greater increase in current density power over time compared to Noise Min epochs.
claims.source: As expected, Noise Max epochs showed a greater increase in current density power over time.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the source localization analysis of the current study.

claims.claim: Significant differences between Noise Max and Noise Min epochs first emerged in the superior parietal cortex from 276 to 304 ms.
claims.source: Significant differences first emerged in the superior parietal cortex (Figure 5d; 276 to 304 ms; tavg(19) = 2.37, pcluster = 0.016, re-emerging at 596 to 748 ms; tavg(19) = 2.53, pcluster = 0.016; and 912 ms; tavg(19) = 2.50, pcluster = 0.014), and then in the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC; 516 to 556 ms; tavg(19) = 2.30, pcluster = 0.022, re-emerging at 660 to 772 ms; tavg(19) = 2.79, pcluster = 0.032, and 824 to 1000 ms; tavg(19) = 2.60, pcluster = 0.022).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the source localization analysis, with reference to Figure 5d.

claims.claim: Significant differences between Noise Max and Noise Min epochs emerged in the orbitofrontal cortex from 516 to 556 ms.
claims.source: Significant differences first emerged in the superior parietal cortex (Figure 5d; 276 to 304 ms; tavg(19) = 2.37, pcluster = 0.016, re-emerging at 596 to 748 ms; tavg(19) = 2.53, pcluster = 0.016; and 912 ms; tavg(19) = 2.50, pcluster = 0.014), and then in the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC; 516 to 556 ms; tavg(19) = 2.30, pcluster = 0.022, re-emerging at 660 to 772 ms; tavg(19) = 2.79, pcluster = 0.032, and 824 to 1000 ms; tavg(19) = 2.60, pcluster = 0.022).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the source localization analysis, with reference to Figure 5d.

claims.claim: No differences in the rostral middle frontal cortex nor lateral occipital cortex survived cluster correction.
claims.source: No differences in the rostral middle frontal cortex nor lateral occipital cortex survived cluster correction.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the source localization analysis of the current study.

claims.claim: Activity localised to the superior parietal cortex reflected stimulus driven computations.
claims.source: Whilst the activity localised to the superior parietal cortex reflected stimulus driven computations (the consecutive peaks correspond temporally to the response to subsequent stimuli), the activity localised to the orbitofrontal cortex was more indicative of an accumulation process across samples (a smoother increase in signal over time).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the temporal dynamics observed in the source localization analysis.

claims.claim: Activity localised to the orbitofrontal cortex was more indicative of an accumulation process across samples.
claims.source: Whilst the activity localised to the superior parietal cortex reflected stimulus driven computations (the consecutive peaks correspond temporally to the response to subsequent stimuli), the activity localised to the orbitofrontal cortex was more indicative of an accumulation process across samples (a smoother increase in signal over time).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the temporal dynamics observed in the source localization analysis.

claims.claim: The activity localised to the orbitofrontal cortex predicted observers' confidence ratings.
claims.source: Indeed, the activity localised to the orbitofrontal cortex predicted observers' confidence ratings, based on the predictions of a generalised linear model with 90/10 cross validation: the standardised regression coefficients increased up to and continued after the perceptual decision response (Figure 5e, a significant cluster was located from −300 to 520 ms around the time of the response; tave(19) = 3.46, cluster-corrected p < 0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the exploratory GLM analysis, with reference to Figure 5e.

claims.claim: Covert decisions could trigger the motor preparation for pressing the response key.
claims.source: This suggests that covert decisions could trigger the motor preparation for pressing the response key.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cross-classification analysis results.

claims.claim: When observers committed to perceptual decisions prematurely, only the early part of the representation of accumulated evidence was attenuated.
claims.source: When observers committed to perceptual decisions prematurely, only the early part of the representation of accumulated evidence was attenuated.

claims.claim: The representations of stimulus orientation and decision update did not substantially change after committing to a perceptual decision.

claims.claim: The P300 and Central Parietal Positivity (CPP) have been found as neural correlates of confidence magnitude related to the accumulation of perceptual decision evidence.
claims.source: Confidence should increase with increasing evidence for the perceptual decision. It is therefore unsurprising that the neural correlates of confidence magnitude have found similar EEG markers as those related to the accumulation of the underlying perceptual decision evidence: the P300 (Gherman and Philiastides, 2015; Desender et al., 2016; Desender et al., 2019; Zakrzewski et al., 2019; Rausch et al., 2020) and Central Parietal Positivity (CPP; Boldt et al., 2019; Herding et al., 2019, indeed we show a similar effect in Appendix 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Confidence is based on information coded in parietal cortex where the underlying perceptual decision evidence is integrated.
claims.source: The difference in superior parietal cortex could be linked with findings from electrophysiology that suggest that confidence is based on information coded in parietal cortex, where the underlying perceptual decision evidence is integrated (Kiani and Shadlen, 2009; Rutishauser et al., 2018; though at least a subset of these neurons reflect bounded accumulation, which is in contrast with the continued confidence accumulation described in this experiment; Kiani et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the current findings to previous electrophysiology studies, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The orbitofrontal cortex has neural coding associated with stimulus value.
claims.source: Early electrophysiological investigation into the function of the orbitofrontal cortex revealed neural coding associated with stimulus value (Thorpe et al., 1983), which has since been linked with a confidence-modulated signal of outcome-expectation (Kepecs et al., 2008; and in human fMRI; Rolls et al., 2010) and recently, shown to be domain-general (single OFC neurons were associated with confidence in both olfactory and auditory tasks; Masset et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Thorpe et al. (1983), Kepecs et al. (2008), Rolls et al. (2010), and Masset et al. (2020).

results.result: Observers commit to perceptual decisions prematurely in the More condition while continuing to accumulate evidence for confidence evaluation. This is demonstrated through behavioral performance showing no significant improvement with additional stimuli (C31-C32), computational modeling revealing a covert bound for perceptual decisions but not confidence (C33-C35), GLM analysis showing differential evidence integration patterns (C38-C40), and motor preparation signatures appearing before the response cue (C43, C72).
results.evaluation: Multiple converging lines of evidence support premature decision commitment: behavioral data (C31-C32), computational modeling with cross-validation (C33-C35), GLM regression analyses (C38-C40), and neural signatures of motor preparation (C43, C72). The statistical tests are appropriate with proper corrections, and the findings replicate prior work (Balsdon et al., 2020).

results.result: Premature decision commitments are revealed by spectral power patterns (8-32 Hz) over motor cortex, with cross-classification showing significantly better accuracy in the More vs Less condition up to 2.5 seconds before response entry. The strength of motor response signals is predicted by accumulated evidence up to four samples prior to response in the More condition.
results.evaluation: The cross-classification analysis with cluster correction (C42) provides strong evidence for early motor preparation. The finding that evidence accumulated up to four samples prior still predicts motor signals in the More condition (C45-C46) supports the interpretation of premature commitment. Statistical tests include appropriate corrections and the approach is methodologically sound.

results.result: Distinct neural representations of stimulus orientation, decision update, and accumulated evidence show different temporal dynamics and topographies. After premature decision commitment, the early representation of accumulated evidence is attenuated (C56, C73) while representations of stimulus orientation and decision update remain unchanged (C57, C74), demonstrating partial dissociation between perceptual and confidence processes.
results.evaluation: The encoding analysis using ridge regression with cross-validation provides robust evidence for distinct representations (C48-C51). The comparison between optimal and suboptimal trials (C52-C55) and between More/Less conditions (C56-C57) with cluster-corrected statistics supports the dissociation. The selective attenuation of accumulated evidence representation after decision commitment is well-demonstrated.

results.result: Bayesian scan statistics identified spatially and temporally distinct clusters for perceptual decisions (early posterior) and confidence evaluation (co-temporal posterior and anterior clusters emerging 668-824 ms post-stimulus). The confidence cluster representation is maintained after decision commitment in the More condition while the perceptual cluster is attenuated, and correlates more strongly with confidence model parameters than perceptual model parameters.
results.evaluation: The Bayesian scan statistics approach provides a principled method for identifying behaviorally relevant signals (C58-C60). The finding that combining clusters improves precision (C61) and the differential maintenance in More condition (C62-C63) with significant interaction (F(1,19)=32.00, p=0.001) strongly support dissociation. The correlation with computational model parameters (C64) validates the functional interpretation.

results.result: Source localization reveals that activity in superior parietal cortex (276-304 ms, stimulus-driven) and orbitofrontal cortex (516-556 ms, accumulation-like) tracks internal evidence for confidence. OFC activity predicts confidence ratings with significant regression weights from -300 to 520 ms around response time.
results.evaluation: Source localization using minimum norm imaging with cluster-corrected comparisons between Noise Max/Min epochs provides robust evidence (C66-C67). The temporal dynamics distinguish stimulus-driven (parietal) from accumulation (OFC) processes (C69-C70). The GLM prediction of confidence ratings from OFC activity (C71) with cross-validation strengthens the functional interpretation. However, source localization from EEG has inherent spatial resolution limitations.

results.result: The optimal presented evidence (accumulated log-likelihood) explains substantial variance in both perceptual decisions (β=0.77, t(19)=6.48, p<0.001) and confidence evaluations (β=0.24, t(19)=6.46, p<0.001).
results.evaluation: The GLM analysis with appropriate statistical tests demonstrates that optimal evidence L predicts both perceptual and confidence responses. The lower beta for confidence is expected given additional noise sources. The analysis validates that observers' internal evidence L* correlates with optimal evidence L.

results.result: The optimal observer computation requires encoding stimulus orientation, estimating decision updates, and accumulating evidence. These variables show distinct temporal dynamics and topographic patterns in EEG.
results.evaluation: The description of optimal computation is well-grounded in prior work (Wyart et al., 2012, 2015). The finding of distinct representations (C48) is supported by the encoding analysis, though this is more of a methodological validation than a primary finding.

results.result: The partial dissociation between perceptual and confidence processes validates computational model predictions and implies a specific neural circuit for confidence computation that can be recruited independently of perceptual processes, potentially enabling metacognitive control.
results.evaluation: While the partial dissociation is well-supported by data (C88), the broader implications about metacognitive control (C86) and general metacognitive mechanisms (C89-C90) are speculative inferences. These claims extend beyond what the current data directly demonstrate and would require additional experiments testing metacognitive control and domain-generality.

results.result: The findings connect to prior literature showing parietal cortex involvement in evidence integration and OFC involvement in confidence-modulated outcome expectation. The results support online confidence computation alongside perceptual accumulation and mediate between single-channel and dual-channel models through partial dissociation.
results.evaluation: These claims appropriately contextualize the current findings within existing literature. The citations are relevant and the interpretations are reasonable. The partial dissociation framework (C85) provides a useful synthesis of competing theoretical models, though this is more interpretive than a direct empirical result.

results.result: Twenty participants completed Free and Replay tasks with oriented Gabor stimuli drawn from overlapping Von Mises distributions. The Replay task manipulated evidence presentation (Less: pmin-2, Same: pmed, More: pmax+4 samples) relative to Free task behavior. No participants were excluded based on pre-registered criteria.
results.evaluation: These methodological details are clearly described and appropriate for the experimental design. The pre-registration (C92) and manipulation based on individual Free task behavior provide good experimental control. Sample size (N=20) is reasonable for within-subject EEG design.

results.result: Background claims establish that perceptual confidence evaluates decision validity, involves metacognitive processes, can integrate post-decisional evidence, may rely on non-perceptual information, and has been linked to prefrontal cortex activity in prior studies. Neural correlates include P300 and CPP signals.
results.evaluation: These are well-established background claims supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. They provide necessary context but are not novel findings from this study. The citations appear accurate and relevant to the claims made.
